text:
Cities Should Stop Forcing Developers to Build Parking

For most of the last century, American cities required developers to build parking before they could build anything else. A new apartment building needed a space for every unit, a restaurant needed a lot sized for its busiest night, and a church needed asphalt for its Sunday crowd. These rules were written with good intentions and very little evidence. They produced places that are expensive to build, hard to walk, and wasteful of land. Cities should remove minimum parking requirements from their planning codes, and they should do it now.

Start with cost. Structured parking is among the most expensive things a developer can build. Underground spaces often cost tens of thousands of dollars each, and that money does not vanish. It is folded into rents and sale prices, so renters and buyers pay for spaces whether or not they own a car. A household that gives up a second vehicle still pays for a space it never uses. Mandated parking raises the price of housing across the board, but the burden falls hardest on low-income households, who are less likely to own cars and most likely to be squeezed out of the neighborhoods with the best transit.

The requirements also fail on their own terms. Minimums are blanket ratios that ignore context. They treat a block beside a subway station the same as a cul-de-sac twenty miles from the nearest bus. They ignore whether tenants are students, seniors, or households that have chosen to live without a car. A single number cannot describe every market, so it produces too much parking in some places and too little in others. Where parking is oversupplied, it sits empty and the land is wasted. Where it is undersupplied, the overflow lands on streets the rules were supposed to protect. Developers who understand their local market already build parking where demand exists. Removing the mandate does not remove parking. It lets the people who pay for it decide how much to buy.

Parking minimums also work against what cities say they want. Most municipal plans now call for more housing, walkable neighborhoods, safer streets, and lively main streets. Every surface lot pushes buildings apart and lengthens the walk between destinations. Every driveway cut interrupts the sidewalk. A ground-floor garage facing the street creates a dead zone where a shop or a stoop should be. Minimum requirements quietly demand the opposite of what the comprehensive plan promises, and they do it through a rule most residents never read.

The strongest objection is that without minimums, streets will fill with cars. That concern deserves a serious answer, not dismissal. But cities that have reduced or eliminated minimums have not seen parking collapse into chaos. Many have kept or added parking maximums, priced on-street spaces so demand matches supply, or created residential permit zones where spillover is a documented problem. These tools are better than a blanket rule because they target the actual problem. If residents need curb space, the answer is to manage the curb, not to force every new building to bury a garage that nobody asked for. Existing residents keep their parking too. The change affects only what new construction must provide.

There is also a question of fairness. Minimums are a subsidy for car ownership, paid for by everyone. Someone who walks, bikes, or rides transit still pays for the garage under their building. Removing minimums moves that cost to the people who choose to drive and makes it visible in their own budget, where it belongs.

Removal will not end car dependence overnight, and no zoning change will fix congestion alone. Some developers will still build parking because lenders, employers, or tenants want it. That is the point. The decision should belong to the people taking the financial risk, not to a rule written decades ago for a city that no longer exists.

Cities have spent decades building rules that assume everyone drives everywhere. The better path is to scrap the mandate, keep the tools that manage curb space and cap excess where necessary, and let builders respond to what residents actually need. That is more honest planning, and it is cheaper for the people who need homes most.
